name: Joseph Stalin
role: Soviet leader and Communist Party general secretary (1922–1953)
summary: Stalin led the Soviet Communist Party from the 1920s until his death in 1953, arguing for socialism in one country, the dictatorship of the proletariat and a single ruling party. In power he collectivised agriculture, ran the economy by a state plan, wrote state ownership, social rights and universal suffrage into the 1936 Constitution, and ruled through mass repression, deportations of whole nationalities, censorship and the Gulag; his social policy banned abortion, recriminalised male homosexuality and promoted large families.

notes: Later pass (claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-10) to rules 5: sources tagged as actions or words, the Wikipedia-only answers re-sourced (abortion, family policy, death penalty, homosexuality, Zhenotdel, workplace democracy, leader cult), candidate statements answered, and record over words applied to his rule (1928-1953): the 1936 Constitution drafted by the commission he chaired, decrees and orders he signed (the 1940 Katyn approval, the 1944 Crimean Tatar deportation decree, the 1939 directive on physical pressure, the Yalta agreements), the laws of his government (1929 religion law, 1931 Glavlit statute, 1934 Kirov decree, 1935 pornography decree, 1936 abortion decree, 1940 labour edict, 1944 family edict, 1947 state-secrets decree of the Council of Ministers he chaired), and reports of his personal role by Khrushchev (1956) and Healey. Constitutional articles answer what the law provided; where his repression contradicts them (secession, equal rights, a bill of rights) the answer is mixed. Themes searched in his collected works (Marxists Internet Archive, about 880 texts saved locally) and the Seventeen Moments in Soviet History documents: ownership, planning, wages and equalisation, work duty, social rights, family, abortion, divorce, religion, nationalities and language, elections and constitution, courts and terror, censorship, war, alliances and territory, revolution, reform and violence, the Comintern. Not covered by his writings or record: drugs, guns, immigration, environment beyond the 1948 nature plan, technology and most modern policy questions, which stay null. The deportations of whole nationalities answer the equal-rights statement; the statements on removing peoples from the country or indigenous peoples from their lands are left null, since the deportations moved them within the USSR.
